solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 24dn.) Accepted victory has gone over Donald's head — a likely blow for a particular region

definitions.text: a likely blow for a particular region

parts.note: the generally accepted opinion is the one that holds sway or is current, the present participle of a verb meaning to win out

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only the opening letter of the name is kept

explanation.surface: A gloating report that Donald Trump's accepted election win has gone over his head.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'gone over' places the victory on top of Donald's first letter. The answer runs across two lights, 1 and 24 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The prevailing wind is the direction from which air most often moves in a given area, so it is the blow most expected there.

clue.text: Martin's inappropriate, getting end away

definitions.note: names the novelist whose surname is the answer

indicators.note: sending the final letter away means the word loses its tail

explanation.surface: A complaint that Martin has behaved inappropriately and got away with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Martin Amis was a British novelist, author of Money and London Fields; dropping the last S of the word for inappropriate gives his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue names the famous writer by first name, and his family name is what the solver must supply.

clue.text: Records about an arse crushing North — and South

indicators.note: to crush something is to squeeze it, so one piece is squeezed inside the other

parts.note: anal means relating to the anus, so concerning an arse
N is the compass abbreviation for North
S is the compass abbreviation for South

explanation.surface: A crude image of someone's backside squashing the North, and the South too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like part of the definition ('records about'), but 'about an arse' as a whole is the adjective that wraps around North.
explanation.definitionFit: Annals are historical records kept year by year, so the word is a synonym for chronicles or records.

clue.text: Trump's last season — needs, er, book of Psalms

indicators.note: the last of something is its final element, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: to season food is to salt it

explanation.surface: Trump in his final season in office needs to hesitate, er, over a hymn book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump's last season' reads as his final year in office, but 'last' takes one letter and 'season' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalter is a volume containing the Psalms, often used in church worship, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Prison label above military establishment

parts.note: pen is US slang for a penitentiary
on can mean placed upon, so above

explanation.surface: A tag stuck above the door of a prison on an army base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Above' looks like a placement word joining label to the definition, but it supplies letters itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pentagon is the headquarters of the US Department of Defense, so it is the best-known military establishment.

clue.text: After surgical procedure with biro, rump's in terrible state — public censure ensues

indicators.note: coming after means placed later in the line, so the shuffled part follows
something in a terrible state is a wreck, so these letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A botched operation leaves a patient's backside scribbled on in pen, and there is a public outcry.
explanation.walkthrough: A biro is a ballpoint pen, used here only for its letters. 'Rump' also hints at Trump, a recurring target in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Opprobrium is harsh criticism or disgrace heaped on someone by the public, a close synonym for censure.

clue.text: see 26dn.
Look back to find Cyclops is being cuddled by sincere drunk

indicators.note: to be cuddled is to be held in someone's arms, so one piece sits inside another
a drunk person staggers about, so the combined letters lurch into a new order

parts.note: the setter Cyclops speaks of himself, so 'Cyclops is' becomes I'M

explanation.surface: The setter being hugged by an earnest drunk and thinking back on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by their pseudonym, so 'Cyclops is' means I am, shortened to I'M; it goes inside the sincere letters before the whole lot is scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: To reminisce is to recall past experiences fondly, which is a way of looking back over time.

clue.text: There's nothing in drink number two

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is enclosed

explanation.surface: A complaint that a second glass has nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number two' reads as a second round of drinks, but it is the childish euphemism.
explanation.definitionFit: Number two is a nursery euphemism for defecation or faeces, and poop is the informal word for the same thing.

clue.text: By way of securing rebellious Democrat finally for Panorama

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece wraps the other
finally points to the end, so only the closing letters of each word are kept

parts.note: the final letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A note that the BBC's Panorama programme secured an interview with a rebellious Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' applies to both words before it, not just Democrat. Panorama is a long-running BBC current affairs programme, hence the capital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A vista is a wide, pleasing view of a landscape, which is what a panorama is too.

clue.text: Low-in-calories, arse on ecstasy learned

parts.note: lite is the marketing spelling for low-calorie food
an arse is a contemptible person, as is a rat
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A dieter, a fool high on ecstasy, is apparently well educated.
explanation.walkthrough: Arse here is the insult for an unpleasant person, not the body part; a rat is a similarly worthless person.
explanation.definitionFit: Literate can mean well read and educated, not merely able to read, so it matches learned as an adjective.

clue.text: Soldiers backing these manoeuvres look like tourists

indicators.note: backing up means going backwards, so the letters run the other way
manoeuvres are moves and repositionings, so these letters are shifted around

explanation.surface: Soldiers supporting these military exercises look like a group of tourists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manoeuvres' fits the military scene as army exercises, which hides its role as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To sightsee is to visit famous places and attractions, the defining activity of a tourist on holiday.

clue.text: Grim, finished, close to how a sulking Trump feels himself to be?

definitions.text: how a sulking Trump feels himself to be

explanation.surface: A gloomy, defeated Trump sulking over how unfairly he has been treated.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is a scenario rather than a dictionary phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hard done by feels unfairly treated, the grievance attributed to a sore loser who sulks.

clue.text: Holding book to use as a basis for action, like Katie Hopkins?

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it in your grasp, so one piece encloses another

parts.words: to use as a basis for action
parts.note: to go by a rule is to act on it
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: Someone clutching a rulebook to justify what they do, rather like a certain loud pundit.
explanation.walkthrough: Katie Hopkins is a British media personality notorious for outspoken, abrasive comments. Gobby is British slang; a gob is a mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Gobby means loud-mouthed and opinionated, so the clue gives an example of such a person rather than a synonym.

clue.text: What Eye crossword solvers have in all good faith — Cyclops!

definitions.text: What Eye crossword solvers have in all good faith
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the polite sign-off on a letter, offered to readers sincerely
second meaning: a jokey way of saying me, the setter

explanation.walkthrough: Eye is Private Eye, the satirical magazine running this puzzle; its setter signs off to solvers and also refers to himself with the same phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase closes formal letters in good faith, and humorously means the speaker himself, here the setter Cyclops.

clue.text: To depart from the script is dregs, atrocious

indicators.note: something atrocious is dreadful and badly made, so these letters are botched into another order

explanation.surface: A critic's verdict that ad-libbing is the dregs of performance, quite atrocious.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an opinion about improvising; the fodder sits right in the middle of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To digress is to wander from the main subject while speaking or writing, leaving the planned text behind.

clue.text: Spot on bottom of alluring girl that gets you visually closer to the action

definitions.text: that gets you visually closer to the action
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun

indicators.note: the bottom of a down word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept

explanation.surface: A blemish on an attractive girl's bottom, seen up close by a voyeur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot on bottom' paints a pimple; in fact spot is a verb and bottom picks a letter, with 'on' placing it above the rest in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A spyglass is a small hand-held telescope, which magnifies distant scenes so that the viewer seems nearer.

clue.text: Outdated Corbyn ultimately in quite a mess

indicators.note: being in something means sitting within it, so one piece is placed inside
a mess is a jumble, so these letters are thrown out of order
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned Jeremy Corbyn ending up in quite a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Corbyn was leader of the UK Labour Party, often mocked as old-fashioned. 'Quite a mess' reads as a phrase but splits into fodder and signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Antique describes something old, and used figuratively it means behind the times, so it matches the adjective.

clue.text: Carry mobile in pursuit of a female? That's not the same thing at all

definitions.text: not the same thing at all

indicators.note: pursuing means following behind, so the shuffled part comes after
something mobile moves about, so these letters shift position

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: Someone protests that carrying a phone while following a woman is nothing like stalking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' reads as a phone being carried, but it is the anagram signal acting on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To say one thing is a far cry from another is an idiom meaning they are very different.

clue.text: Scatterbrained insult about unfilled 24 hours

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the letters face the other way

parts.note: a dig is a snide remark

indicators.note: something unfilled is empty inside, so only the outside letters remain

parts.note: 24 hours is a day, emptied of its middle

explanation.surface: A dizzy person insulted about wasting an empty day.
explanation.walkthrough: '24 hours' looks like it points to clue 24, but it is simply a day.
explanation.definitionFit: Giddy describes someone flighty, frivolous and excitable, a near synonym for a scatterbrained person.

clue.text: Cardinal's soft — more when pissed

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order

explanation.surface: A churchman who goes even softer after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: Cardinal looks like the Catholic prelate, but it is the adjective; the dash in the fodder is just punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal as an adjective means chief or of primary importance, as in cardinal sin, so it equals leading.

clue.text: Celebrity place known for divorce and welcome new beginnings

parts.note: Reno, Nevada, was famous for quick divorces

indicators.note: beginnings are starts, so only the opening letters of the words are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of welcome and new

explanation.surface: A famous resort where stars go to divorce and happily start over.
explanation.walkthrough: Reno in Nevada had lax residency rules that made it the divorce capital of the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrity in its abstract sense means fame or wide public recognition, which is exactly what renown is.

clue.text: Liberal Les, full of gas, associated with Republican cheat

indicators.note: being associated means joined alongside, so one piece is attached to the next
being full of something means holding it inside
something liberal is free and loose, so these letters are freely rearranged

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A windbag Liberal politician called Les teaming up with a Republican fraudster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' reads as a party label for Les, but it is the anagram signal; 'full of gas' suggests a windbag.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindler cheats people out of money or property by deception, so the noun is a synonym for cheat.

clue.text: see 1dn.
Country gets Farage to change political allegiance?

indicators.note: switching allegiance means swapping left for right, so one letter is exchanged for another

parts.note: Nigel Farage, the British right-wing politician

explanation.surface: A nation tempts Nigel Farage to defect to another party.
explanation.walkthrough: L and R are the abbreviations for left and right, so changing political side swaps the final L for R.
explanation.definitionFit: Niger is a landlocked nation in West Africa, so the general word for a state covers it.

clue.text: (& 7dn.) Person who's quite acceptable to dogs or bats

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so these letters go wild into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone liked by dogs, or by bats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogs or bats' reads as two animals; bats is the slang adjective for crazy. The answer spans 26 and 7 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A good sort is an informal British phrase for a decent, likeable person, someone others find agreeable.

clue.text: Cold-shoulder American arse on the rebound

indicators.note: something on the rebound bounces back the way it came

parts.note: buns is US slang for buttocks

explanation.surface: Ignoring an American jerk who is on the rebound from a breakup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rebound' paints someone fresh from a relationship, but it signals the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: To cold-shoulder someone is to ignore them deliberately, which is exactly what it means to snub them.

clue.text: Post-war organisation repeated large test of opinion

indicators.note: organising things means putting them in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: A post-war body repeatedly running a big opinion survey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post-war organisation' reads as something like the UN; organisation is the anagram signal working on the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A straw poll is an informal, unofficial vote taken to gauge general feeling on a question.
